https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/08/roma.text: Menü Kereső Kövekkel megpakolt uszályokat süllyesztettek el Romániában, hogy tovább működhessen az atomerőmű Külföld Gazdaság Thüringer Barbara Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Több, kővel megrakott uszályt süllyesztettek Romániában a Duna medrébe a cernavodai atomerőmű még működő kettes blokkjának üzemben tartása érdekében – közölte szombaton a News.ro hírportálra hivatkozva az MTI. Az erős áramlások miatt több ízben elhalasztott műveletet pénteken kezdték meg a Cernavodától 60 kilométernyire található elágazásnál. Szombat hajnalig két uszály ellenőrzött elárasztását fejezték be. A hatóságok ezáltal mesterséges víz alatti padkát emelnek a Bala-ág medrében, hogy több vizet tereljenek a másik ágra, az erőmű felé vezető Öreg-Dunába. A tervek szerint szombat délután újabb két uszályt süllyesztenek el. Szombaton az előző napinál 4 centiméterrel alacsonyabb, mínusz 222 centiméteres vízállást mértek Cernavodánál. A mostani vízszabályozási beavatkozásoktól az apadás ideiglenes megállítását, illetve késleltetését remélik, amivel 3-4 nappal elodázhatják az atomerőmű teljes lekapcsolását. Amennyiben a vízállás eléri a mínusz 233 centiméteres szintet, az atomerőmű 700 megawattos kettes blokkját is le kell állítani. A Duna vízhozama szerdán süllyedt a négy évtizede feljegyzett, másodpercenként 1400 köbméteres történelmi mélypontra a romániai szakasz belépő pontján, Báziásnál. A vízügyi hatóságok szerint augusztus 14-ig nem várható jelentős változás, azt követően enyhe emelkedésre számítanak. A román kormány múlt héten készenléti állapotot hirdetett a Duna alacsony vízállása és az energiahiány miatt, pénteken pedig felhatalmazta a villamosenergia-hálózat üzemeltetőjét, hogy szükség esetén lekapcsolja a nagy ipari fogyasztókat. A Duna magyarországi szakaszán már emelkedésnek indult a vízszint az elmúlt napokban. Szombaton a Duna vízállása Paksnál -127 centiméter volt, a következő napokra pedig azt várják a vízügyi szakemberek, hogy akár visszatérhet a korábban mért legkisebb vízállási vízszintre , vagyis -97 centire is a folyó vízállása. Ugyanakkor a folyó vízhőmérséklete Paksnál jelenleg 28,3 Celsius fok, emiatt folyamatosan monitorozni kell a folyót, hogy az atomerőmű hűtése során ne károsodjon a folyó élővilága. https://www.businessday.co.za/news/law/2.text: Law Taxi boss Msibi tried to buy R14.8m phone surveillance device Madlanga commission hears Fannie Nkosi used SAPS authority to facilitate a device demonstration August 18, 2026 5 min read Share current article via Email Share current article via Facebook Share current article via Twitter Share current article via LinkedIn Sinesipho Schrieber Journalist Opens in new window Opens in new window Opens in new window Opens in new window Enter fullscreen mode displaying this image. Expand The late taxi boss Jothan Msibi in the spotlight at the Madlanga commission of inquiry . (Business Times) Story audio is generated using AI In a clear example of the alleged infiltration of the police by criminal elements, Sgt Fannie Nkosi used his official stamp and position to facilitate the potential acquisition of cellphone-surveillance equipment by the late alleged crime kingpin and taxi warlord Jothan Msibi. Chats downloaded from Msibi’s phone were presented as evidence at the Madlanga commission, which is investigating allegations that corrupt elements have infiltrated the country’s criminal justice system. The late Msibi was previously identified at the commission as the leader of the “Big Five cartel”. Nkosi, alleged runner of suspended deputy national commissioner Lt-Gen Shadrack Sibiya , is under arrest and facing other charges of money-laundering and defeating the ends of justice. His role in this deal could see him facing more charges. On Tuesday, chief evidence leader for the commission Matthew Chaskalson showed retired justice Mbuyisile Madlanga and his co-commissioners advocates Sesi Baloyi and Sandile Khumalo a letter addressed to the Czech Republic’s ministry of industry and trade in February 2023. The chat detailed arrangements of a possible demonstration of the international mobile subscriber identity (IMSI) catchers, arranged to be made at the SAPS head offices in Pretoria. A letter to authorise a foreign company, Invasys, to do the demonstration was signed and stamped by Nkosi. The devices, colloquially known in the intelligence world as “grabbers”, can be used to spy on and download cellphone communications. Chaskalson said Nkosi stamped the letter for Invasys to create the impression that the demonstration of the spying devices would be for authorised users — law enforcement officers. A letter signed by police officer Fannie Nkosi sent to the Czech Republic. Picture: Madlanga Commission (Madlanga commission of inquiry ) The Invasys company website states that it is “a research and development company dedicated to empowering governments with advanced security technologies to counter terrorism, insurgency and organised crime”. Evidence shows Nkosi signed the letter knowing that the demonstration would not be for police but for taxi boss Msibi, who seemingly wanted to sell the technology system to the Eswatini government. “The Czech Republic was told this is a demonstration to the SAPS,” Chaskalson said, adding Nkosi’s actions amounted to fraud. According to the chats, Chaskalson said Msibi, murder accused Katiso Molefe and security company boss Steve Motsumi apparently planned to have a business venture that sold the devices. Chats between Nkosi and Shaun Jacobs, who was the middleman for Invasys, show the talks started in January 2023, and two of its representatives, Ivan Vercueil and Thomas Jensen, visited the country in February to demonstrate the devices. “Hi Fani, we need the company name for the contract with Invasys and the email address; we need to send the contract too! This will come directly to the Czech company. This way, Ubaba [Msibi] will be protected if anyone tries to go behind his back,” Jacobs said in a message sent to Nkosi in February 2023. In March 7 2023, when Jacobs inquired whether the deal was on track, Nkosi indicated Msibi was meeting “the king”. “Yes, tomorrow morning the king is having a final meeting with the old man [Msibi],” Nkosi said. The deal communicated by Nkosi with Jacobs for the devices collapsed in October 2023. Commissioner Sandile Khumalo asked Chaskalson what the commission was to make of Nkosi signing documents purporting to be acting on behalf of the SAPS and sending them to foreign agencies. “It is an outright fraud,” said Chaskalson. The commission has not yet traced Jacobs. “We see one instance where he [Nkosi] is signing and putting a stamp to allow an international organisation to make a demonstration to private individuals in South Africa. What if it was weapons and other things not authorised by the SAPS?” Khumalo asked. It is an outright fraud. — Matthew Chaskalson, chief evidence leader for the commission The evidence before the commission suggests the collapsed deal with the Czech company was not Msibi’s last attempt to get into the spying device business. Flight records show Msibi and security company boss Motsumi flew to Frankfurt, Germany, and thereafter to Paris on May 16 2023. WhatsApp chats show that during travel, Msibi sent to Motsumi a profile of the company Themy Style. “Company vision: To be No 1 trusted intelligence security services in Southern Africa and beyond,” the company profile reads. The document shows Msibi and Molefe, who is facing trial for the assassination of engineer Armand Swart, as directors. Official records, however, show Msibi was the only registered director of the company. The company outlined its mission was providing covert operations (secret operations carried out by government or military), protection services, private detectives and technical surveillance — and provided services to the “state”. During the trip, an email by a Nokuthula Nxumalo to a European dealer in high-technology security surveillance equipment purported that Msibi and Motsumi were representing Thyme Style and had security contracts with the “state”. The email did not identify which state. A few days after the trip to Germany and France, on May 23 2023, Msibi received a quotation for multiradio access technology BTS (grabber) indicated to cost €780,000 (R14.8m) per unit. The quotation also included prices for a digital jammer, which blocks cellphone signals. “These three men [Msibi, Motsumi and Molefe] are dealing with foreign companies to get access to grabber technology, purporting to represent a state,” Chaskalson said. “What we are looking at here is quite alarming. Messrs Msibi, Motsumi, Molefe and possibly Sgt Nkosi are involved in a commercial project. “This is a worrying state of affairs. This is the sort of technology that should only go into the hands of intelligence agencies who are then constrained to use it under very strict legislative control. What we have here is private parties.” Whether the deal with the European dealer went through was unclear from the evidence before the commission, Chaskalson said. Evidence before the commission shows Msibi was a powerful figure. He was known by top cops, including Lt-Gen Shadrack Sibiya, and many politicians, including Julius Malema. His phone records show he also communicated with former Ekurhuleni city manager Imogen Mashazi. He was also linked to North West businessperson Suliman Carrim . https://jamestown.org/hungarys-ukraine-r.text: Hungary’s Ukraine Reset Off to a Shaky Start Foreign Policy Publication Eurasia Daily Monitor Hungary 10.06.2026 Péter Fazekas Top Stories Russian Black Sea Fleet Intrudes Bulgarian Waters, Harasses Turkish Grain Freighter Foreign Policy Russia’s Combat Losses in Ukraine Deduced From Rosstat’s ‘Unassigned Deaths’ Category Military & Security Russia Exhausts Soviet-Era Arms Storage Bases Military & Security Hungary’s Ukraine Reset Off to a Shaky Start Executive Summary: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar initially aimed for a quick reset with Ukraine by unblocking Kyiv’s EU accession talks in exchange for a bilateral deal on protecting and expanding the rights of ethnic Hungarians in Ukraine. The bilateral relationship has seen major setbacks in recent weeks over Hungary’s refusal to advance Ukraine’s EU accession talks, Magyar saying that a Ukrainian petroleum storage facility would not be built in Hungary under Tisza rule, and Budapest’s decision not to join the Carpathian Eight, a new Ukraine-led regional cooperation format. Future Hungary–Ukraine relations will be defined by Ukraine’s implementation of the minority rights agreement, with legislative progress expected in October. A failure to implement the deal could risk slowing down Kyiv’s EU path and decoupling the Ukrainian and Moldovan accession bids. Hungary blocked progress on Ukrainian EU accession on September 8 for the fourth time since the first negotiating cluster opened on June 15. Hungarian diplomats said Budapest’s approval of new negotiating clusters is contingent on Kyiv’s implementation of commitments protecting the rights of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine’s Zakarpattia oblast ( Index , September 9). Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry responded that Hungary should not make the implementation of minority-rights commitments a condition for opening unrelated negotiation clusters. Kyiv argues that it already incorporated the commitments into its action plan, the execution of which the European Union will evaluate as a part of the accession process ( Shelter , September 21). This incident demonstrates that Budapest’s Ukraine policy under Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar may be contingent on Ukraine’s approach to the rights of its Hungarian minority. Hungary’s continued refusal to advance Ukraine’s EU membership talks is the latest manifestation of Budapest’s evolving Ukraine policy under the country’s new government. After Magyar’s Tisza party defeated Russian-friendly Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party in April parliamentary elections, the new pro-EU government vowed to restore Hungary’s relations with the European Union and North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO). Magyar subsequently downgraded diplomatic and political relations with Russia (see EDM , April 15). This new government has offered Ukraine an opportunity to reset ties with Hungary after years of anti-Ukrainian policy and rhetoric under Viktor Orbán’s consecutive governments from 2010–2026 (see EDM , March 25). Only a month after Hungary’s new government was installed in May, Magyar announced a surprise agreement between Budapest and Kyiv. Under the deal, Hungary dropped its opposition to opening new EU accession negotiating clusters with Ukraine in exchange for comprehensive legislative reforms protecting and expanding the cultural, educational, and language rights of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine. Ukraine committed to restoring the system of schools for national minorities, allowing the use of Hungarian in education and school communications. In settlements where the proportion of the Hungarian population exceeds 10 percent, Kyiv will also allow the free use of Hungarian national symbols. Disagreements about how implementation of this “historic agreement” should be evaluated flared in recent weeks. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry insisted progress should be assessed through existing EU accession mechanisms and not via new conditions from Hungary. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sibyha said the previous Hungarian government’s policies of “obstructionism and isolationism continue to thrive,” blocking Ukraine’s EU path ( Népszava , September 22). At the same time, Kyiv emphasized that the deal’s educational reforms will be implemented by the end of this year, and legislation on the remaining issues will be passed by May 2027 ( Karpat.in.ua , September 22). Following weeks of uncertainty, Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced that Budapest and Kyiv resolved the misunderstandings after a series of meetings with her Ukrainian counterpart during the UN General Assembly High-level Week. The Hungarian foreign minister expects legislative progress on the Hungarian minority in Ukraine by the end of October ( Index , September 24). On October 2, Magyar welcomed Ukraine submitting draft legislation on Hungarian educational rights to the Verkhovna Rada, Ukraine’s parliament ( HVG , October 2). The Verkhovna Rada is expected to vote on the bill on October 12 ( Evropeis’ka Pravda , October 6). On September 21, Magyar, a critic of Ukraine’s fast-track EU accession, said that Hungary is not participating in a new regional cooperation format launched by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that would include Austria, Czechia, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, and Ukraine. Dubbed the Carpathian Eight, its inaugural regional summit was held on September 18. Romanian President Nicușor Dan, Polish President Donald Tusk, and then-Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić were present, while Budapest was only represented by Hungary’s chargé d’affaires to Kyiv. Following the summit, however, the Hungarian foreign minister did not rule out the possibility of Budapest joining the forum in the future. Magyar’s post-summit comments may have been fueled by a memorandum signed by Ukraine’s Naftogaz and Hungarian oil company MOL on the sidelines of the gathering to explore the construction of Ukrainian petroleum-product storage facilities in Hungary near the border. Magyar said the negotiations between the two oil companies were started under the previous Orbán-led government and criticized MOL for continuing negotiations without informing his government. He also said that no Ukrainian storage facility would be built in Hungary while Tisza is in power ( 444 , September 22). The Hungarian government owns a 25 percent stake in MOL and has said that it is unacceptable that the company conducted negotiations with the Ukrainian government-owned Naftogaz without Budapest’s consent. Combined, these developments signal that Magyar is consciously keeping himself away from Ukrainian affairs. Ukraine and Hungary have repeatedly discussed dates and locations for a formal bilateral summit between Zelenskyy and Magyar that has still not taken place. Advancing Ukraine’s EU accession bid without tangible results in protecting ethnic Hungarians would directly undermine Magyar’s pre-election promises, erode support for Tisza, and provide Orbán’s Fidesz–KDNP with fuel for attacks. Hungary’s new ruling party operates in an environment that was shaped by years of Orbán-driven anti-Ukrainian narratives, and most of the Hungarian population has an unfavorable view of Ukraine ( 24.hu , December 19, 2025). Public sentiment could be the primary reason why Magyar is criticizing Kyiv for not implementing an agreement that is supposed to be completed later. Employing tough rhetoric against Kyiv may also be intended to retain the Ukraine-skeptic part of the Tisza voter base and gain the sympathy of some right-wing opposition voters. In parallel, this signals that Hungary’s Ukraine approach has a dual track that combines tough rhetoric from the prime minister with more conciliatory negotiations led by the foreign minister. While some observers see Hungary’s opposition to advancing Ukraine’s EU bid as a continuation of Hungary’s Orbán-era Ukraine policy, the new government promised pragmatic bilateral relations focused on protecting Hungarian interests while also affirming a Western orientation. Even with recent setbacks, the contrast with the Orbán era remains notable because of the new government’s decision to unblock EU aid to Ukraine and the opening of new EU membership talks in June. In the coming months, a full implementation of the minority rights agreement could pave the way for the opening of two of the remaining four EU accession negotiation clusters. In contrast, a Ukrainian failure to implement these changes or other bilateral disputes will risk slowing down the Ukrainian accession bid or even decoupling it from Moldova’s. Hungary has no opposition to advancing the Moldovan application, but the European Union has linked Ukrainian and Moldovan accession through its “package approach.” Even after the accession talks end, Ukraine’s entry into the organization—as Magyar has repeatedly stated—could come down to a Hungarian referendum, the outcome of which is uncertain.
